DecisionUnlearn-Bench: Unlearning Probabilistic Decisions under Changing Schemas

Tiantong Wu Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore Correspondence to: tiantong.wu@ntu.edu.sg    Wei Yang Bryan Lim Affiliation: Nanyang Technological University, Singapore
Abstract

Machine unlearning aims to reproduce the behavior of a model trained without designated data. For probabilistic decision models, this target also depends on the candidate options supplied at inference. We introduce DecisionUnlearn-Bench, an empirical framework that compares full, unlearned, and retain-only models across deletion granularities, label renderings, and candidate sets. Across 20 eligible model configurations on the BANKING77 dataset, full-to-oracle displacement increases consistently from example to association to class deletion. Replacing semantic option labels with opaque codes nearly eliminates the retrained oracle’s recognition of deleted classes, even with successful acquisition of the full model, whereas changing the candidate set alters both the oracle and the measured unlearning progress. SimNPO satisfies the screening criterion in 19 of 20 configurations, but its gains vary substantially across seeds and deletion targets. Development tuning on the CLINC150 dataset does not establish a positive pooled effect across 48 intents. At approximately matched suppression, methods can differ markedly in oracle fidelity. Recovery experiments further distinguish initial forgetting from subsequent adaptation and show conclusions that depend on both architecture and metric. These results show that evaluating decision-model unlearning relative to a schema-specific retraining target, with separate reporting of effect size, utility, robustness, and recoverability.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Machine unlearning asks how to remove the influence of designated training data in a trained model without repeating the entire training process (Ginart et al., 2019; Bourtoule et al., 2021). A central reference is the model obtained by training on the remaining data. This reference makes the objective more precise than simply reducing accuracy on examples associated with a deletion request. A relevant question is whether the unlearned model would have behaved the same way without those examples.

This distinction matters for models that return probabilities over a specified set of decisions. For example, in intent classification, a request is evaluated against a set of named candidate intents. The model can use both its learned mapping from utterances to intents and the meanings of the supplied labels. Removing every training sample of an intent therefore need not eliminate recognition of that intent. The remaining data, pretrained knowledge, and candidate descriptions may still support the correct decision.

Existing language-model unlearning benchmarks examine forgotten knowledge, retained utility, privacy, and robustness through complementary evaluations (Maini et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025; Dorna et al., 2026). Preference-based methods also address the instability of directly maximizing the loss on data that needs to be forgotten (Zhang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). These developments leave an additional evaluation question for decision models:

How should fidelity to retraining be interpreted when the information supplied by the decision schema changes?

A low forgotten-class accuracy can agree with one retraining target and disagree with another. Similarly, a normalized improvement can change because the unlearned model changes, the oracle changes, or the original deletion effect becomes small.

Three distinctions are consequently necessary. First, the counterfactual effect of deletion must be measured before interpreting an intervention. Second, the amount of probability removed from forgotten options must be separated from where that probability is redistributed. Third, high performance after further adaptation must be separated from the behavior already present before adaptation. Without these distinctions, a method can appear to forget successfully, transfer reliably, or relearn rapidly for reasons that the reported endpoint does not isolate.

We address these questions with DecisionUnlearn-Bench, a study of probabilistic decision unlearning on the BANKING77 and CLINC150 datasets (Casanueva et al., 2020; Larson et al., 2019). The benchmark compares a full model, an unlearned model, and a retain-only retrained oracle using their complete option distributions. It separates: (i) example, association, and class deletion, (ii) development selection and subsequent evaluation, and (iii) broad model screening and targeted replication. Controlled changes to label rendering and candidate composition test how the decision interface changes the target itself.

The results identify both useful approximation and clear limits. Class deletion creates the largest distributional shift across all models in the 20-model granularity panel. SimNPO provides reliable gains across the reference BANKING77 seed-bundle grid, yet its performance under the frozen setting is less stable across other seeds and across CLINC150 targets. Opaque labels almost eliminate oracle recognition, but do not consistently increase normalized unlearning progress. Reduced candidate sets can also expose poor fidelity when labels are opaque, showing that schema sensitivity extends beyond residual semantic recognition. Recovery analyses produce different conclusions for Apertus-8B and Qwen3.5-9B models once starting behavior and remaining headroom are separated.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    An evaluation design that measures displacement and approximation induced by deletion to a retraining target specific to the schema on both deleted training rows and unseen related rows.

  • •

    An empirical account of how label semantics and candidate composition alter oracle behavior and the interpretation of unlearning fidelity.

  • •

    A combined analysis of method transfer, probability redistribution, and recovery that separates statistical acceptance from effect size and identifies the limits of conclusions drawn from a fixed decision interface.

2 Related Work

Unlearning as approximation to retraining.

Data-deletion formulations and efficient retraining schemes establish the importance of specifying the learning procedure whose output is to be reproduced (Ginart et al., 2019; Bourtoule et al., 2021). More recent oracle-matching approaches explicitly target output distributions rather than only the correctness of forgotten predictions (Georgiev et al., 2025). We adopt retraining as an operational reference for supervised task adaptation. Our experiments do not remove the dataset from the pre-training or establish equality between the distributions over the trained model parameters.

Language-model unlearning methods and evaluation.

TOFU (Maini et al., 2024) studies synthetic author knowledge with retain-only references, whereas MUSE (Shi et al., 2025) evaluates several aspects of forgetting and retained utility. The OpenUnlearning (Dorna et al., 2026) framework consolidates these two methods and evaluations to examine the reliability across different metrics. NPO (Zhang et al., 2024) and SimNPO (Fan et al., 2025) modify the forgetting objective to improve optimization behavior. RMU (li2024wmdp) instead intervenes on internal representations. Our contribution is an empirical investigation of these approaches in a decision setting, rather than a new unlearning optimizer.

Decision schemas and recoverability.

Intent datasets provide explicit candidate meanings and natural distinctions between removing individual records and removing all examples of an intent (Casanueva et al., 2020; Larson et al., 2019). We vary those candidate meanings and the supplied option set while retaining the same evaluation inputs. Relearning is already an established unlearning evaluation, including in the SimNPO study (Fan et al., 2025). Here, it compares adaptation from unlearned and retrained checkpoints while distinguishing starting-point differences, subsequent gains, and transfer through a newly initialized head.

3 Problem Formulation and Evaluation

3.1 A schema-specific retraining target

Let 𝒟\mathcal{D} be the supervised training set, 𝒟ℱ⊂𝒟\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}\subset\mathcal{D} a deletion set, and 𝒟ℛ=𝒟∖𝒟ℱ\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{R}}=\mathcal{D}\setminus\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}} the retained set. A decision schema 𝒮=(𝒞,ℓ)\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{C},\ell) specifies an ordered candidate set 𝒞\mathcal{C} and its textual rendering ℓ\ell, including option names and descriptions. Model MM returns a categorical distribution

𝐩M​(x,𝒮)=(pM​(c∣x;𝒮))c∈𝒞,∑c∈𝒞pM​(c∣x;𝒮)=1.\mathbf{p}_{M}(x;\mathcal{S})=\bigl(p_{M}(c\mid x;\mathcal{S})\bigr)_{c\in\mathcal{C}},\qquad\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}}p_{M}(c\mid x;\mathcal{S})=1. (1)

The term decision model refers to this probabilistic interface throughout the paper.

For a training procedure 𝒜\mathcal{A}, pretrained initialization M0M_{0}, and training seed ξ\xi, we compare

Mfull\displaystyle M_{\mathrm{full}} =𝒜⁡(M0,𝒟,𝒮train,ξ),\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}(M_{0},\mathcal{D},\mathcal{S}_{\rm train};\xi), (2)
M𝒪\displaystyle M_{\mathcal{O}} =𝒜⁡(M0,𝒟ℛ,𝒮train,ξ),\displaystyle=\mathcal{A}(M_{0},\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{R}},\mathcal{S}_{\rm train};\xi),
M𝒰\displaystyle M_{\mathcal{U}} =𝒰⁡(Mfull,𝒟ℱ,𝒟ℛ),\displaystyle=\mathcal{U}(M_{\mathrm{full}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}},\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{R}}),

where 𝒰\mathcal{U} denotes an approximate unlearning procedure. The retrained oracle M𝒪M_{\mathcal{O}} is trained without the deletion set under the task-training recipe. The no-op baseline is MfullM_{\mathrm{full}}. Both references are evaluated under the same schema as M𝒰M_{\mathcal{U}}. In particular, deleted classes remain available as options: deleting their training examples does not remove their outputs from the decision space.

The label intervention changes 𝒮train\mathcal{S}_{\rm train} and the corresponding evaluation rendering, requiring separately trained full and oracle models. The candidate-set intervention changes the evaluation schema of existing checkpoints and performs a new forward pass for each reduced option set. These interventions address different sources of schema dependence.

3.2 Deletion granularity and evaluation views

We study three deletion requests. (i) Example deletion removes a random 5% of training rows. (ii) Association deletion removes selected sub-intent clusters while retaining other examples of their parent intents. And (iii) Class deletion removes all training rows of selected classes. The primary BANKING77 comparison uses ten association clusters or four classes, whereas CLINC150 class bundles contain eight intents.

We distinguish two evaluation views. The (i) forget-training view ℰℱ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}} contains deleted training rows. The (ii) forget-generalization view ℰ𝒢\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}} contains unseen evaluation rows associated with the deleted units. For class and association deletion, these are rows of the corresponding class or cluster. For example deletion, these are evaluation rows whose nearest training row belongs to 𝒟ℱ\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}. Thus, 𝒢\mathcal{G} does not denote a second deletion set or a generic robustness benchmark. Retained utility is evaluated on ℰℛ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{R}}.

3.3 Distance, progress, and feasibility

For v∈{ℱ,𝒢}v\in\{\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}\}, the oracle distance is the mean base-2 Jensen–Shannon divergence:

ODv⁡(M;𝒮)=1|ℰv|​∑x∈ℰvJS2⁡(𝐩M​(x,𝒮),𝐩M𝒪​(x,𝒮)).\operatorname{OD}_{v}(M;\mathcal{S})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}_{v}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{E}_{v}}\operatorname{JS}_{2}\!\left(\mathbf{p}_{M}\left(x;\mathcal{S}\right),\mathbf{p}_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}\left(x;\mathcal{S}\right)\right). (3)

We use raw option probabilities, with numerical stabilization at 10−1210^{-12}. We define

D0,v\displaystyle D_{0,v} =ODv⁡(Mfull;𝒮),\displaystyle=\operatorname{OD}_{v}(M_{\mathrm{full}};\mathcal{S}), (4)
Δ​ODv\displaystyle\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{v} =D0,v−ODv⁡(M𝒰;𝒮),\displaystyle=D_{0,v}-\operatorname{OD}_{v}(M_{\mathcal{U}};\mathcal{S}),
Pv\displaystyle P_{v} =Δ​ODvD0,v=1−ODv⁡(M𝒰,𝒮)D0,v.\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{v}}{D_{0,v}}=1-\frac{\operatorname{OD}_{v}(M_{\mathcal{U}};\mathcal{S})}{D_{0,v}}.

Here D0,vD_{0,v} is deletion displacement, Δ​ODv\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{v} is the absolute gain over no-op, and PvP_{v} is normalized oracle progress. Positive gain means closer agreement with the oracle. Progress equals zero for no-op and one for exact agreement on the evaluated distributions, and negative values indicate movement away from the oracle. Because the denominator depends on the deletion request and schema, we report D0,vD_{0,v} and absolute gains alongside progress. We do not interpret ratios with negligible displacement as stable effect sizes.

A configuration is feasible when retained accuracy decreases by at most 0.02 and retained expected calibration error increases by at most 0.02 relative to the corresponding full model:

Accℛ⁡(M𝒰)≥Accℛ⁡(Mfull)−0.02,ℰ​C​Eℛ​(M𝒰)≤ℰ​C​Eℛ​(Mfull)+0.02.\begin{split}\operatorname{Acc}_{\mathcal{R}}(M_{\mathcal{U}})\geq\operatorname{Acc}_{\mathcal{R}}(M_{\mathrm{full}})-0.02,\\ \mathcal{E}CE_{\mathcal{R}}(M_{\mathcal{U}})\leq\mathcal{E}CE_{\mathcal{R}}(M_{\mathrm{full}})+0.02.\end{split} (5)

Protocol acceptance additionally requires positive gains with positive lower 95% confidence bounds on both views. It specifies no minimum progress fraction and does not imply equivalence to retraining.

3.4 Selection, replication, and uncertainty

Development data determine target eligibility, method configurations, and suppression matching. Primary class targets require full-model development accuracy of at least 0.70 and gold probability of at least 0.50. Association targets use an accuracy threshold of 0.65. Targets are selected in hash order among eligible units at the primary seed. Replication preserves target selection rather than silently replacing difficult seed-specific cases. One semantic BANKING77 bundle-02 class falls below the accuracy threshold at seed 42. We disclose this exception in Appendix B.

Within a fixed trained configuration, estimates use 5000 paired row-bootstrap draws, with forgotten-class or association-cluster bootstraps as sensitivity analyses. Each progress ratio is recomputed inside the resample. The frozen confirmation family reports Holm-adjusted intersection–union tests based on the larger of the two one-sided view-specific pp-values. Architecture-screening decisions use the stored per-model rule without correction across models. Reference-model cross-bundle summaries use the stored hierarchical bootstrap over seeds, bundles, and units. Row intervals are conditioned on trained checkpoints and do not quantify uncertainty over future training seeds.

4 Experimental Design

BANKING77 provides 77 fine-grained banking intents, while CLINC150 spans 150 in-scope intents across ten domains (Casanueva et al., 2020; Larson et al., 2019). Our CLINC150 interface contains 151 options, including out-of-scope options. The model panel contains 20 eligible configurations. InternLM3-8B was excluded because checkpoint reloading was not reproducible. Qwen3.5-0.8B is the reference model for method selection and the most extensive replication. We use model configuration to denote a named backbone and its size. Multiple configurations can belong to the same model family.

We evaluate gradient ascent (GradAscent), gradient difference with retained-data supervision (GradDiff), its KL-regularized variant (GradDiff-KL), NPO, SimNPO, RMU, and a uniformization control in the experimental blocks, each of which was selected or specified. These are not a complete method-by-model factorial comparison. The main confirmation compares six class-deletion arms, with the broad transfer panel evaluating the frozen reference-model SimNPO configuration. RMU is included in the suppression diagnostic. Temperature scaling provides an additional control for CLINC150.

The main evaluation design separates three questions. First, the granularity screen measures the changes in retain-only retraining across all eligible models. Second, method confirmation and a seed-bundle replication test approximate that target. Third, schema, suppression, and recovery interventions examine why a favorable fixed-interface result may not persist. Table 1 summarizes observed evaluation coverage. Supplementary tables preserve the full numerical results and the detailed distinction among the pilot, development, confirmation, screening, replication, and exploratory stages.

5 Results

5.1 Deletion granularity determines the size of the counterfactual shift

Full-to-oracle displacement increases from example to association, then to class deletion in every configuration in the BANKING77 screen (Figure 1). The panel medians are respectively 0.035, 0.150, and 0.477 on ℱ\mathcal{F}, and 0.021, 0.149, and 0.396 on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. These are descriptive medians over model configurations, not population estimates.

Same-data replicas are available for Qwen3.5-0.8B at seeds 17, 42, and 99. For this model, example-deletion displacement is approximately within twice the observed replica noise. This supports the protocol’s decision not to advance example-deletion methods beyond selection. It does not establish that deleted records were never memorized, or that retaining the full model meets a privacy requirement. The replica comparison is also specific to this reference model.

Association deletion produces a larger target shift, and its final cross-bundle sensitivity analysis finds modest SimNPO gains: Δ​ODℱ=0.019\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{F}}=0.019 [0.007,0.034][0.007,0.034] and Δ​OD𝒢=0.018\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{G}}=0.018 [0.005,0.035][0.005,0.035]. We retain this result while distinguishing its selection pathway from the primary class-deletion confirmation. The strongest and most extensively replicated intervention evidence concerns class deletion.

5.2 Label meaning changes the oracle, but does not guarantee easier unlearning

We replace option names and descriptions with fixed opaque codes while preserving utterances, target identities, option order, and the availability of forgotten options. Full models pass the opaque-label acquisition checks. On BANKING77, oracle accuracy on deleted training rows falls from 0.209–0.315 with semantic labels to zero across both bundles and both seeds. The corresponding unseen-row accuracies are also zero under opaque labels. Forgotten-option mass remains small but nonzero, approximately 4.7×10−44.7\times 10^{-4} to 1.8×10−31.8\times 10^{-3} on ℱ\mathcal{F} (Figure 2A,B).

The CLINC150 contrasts show the same qualitative oracle effect. Semantic-label oracle accuracy on ℱ\mathcal{F} is 0.661, 0.505, and 0.781 for bundles 02, 03, and 06. With opaque labels, only one of 791 rows is correct on bundle 02, and none is correct on bundles 03 or 06. Full-to-oracle displacement increases to 0.983, 0.993, and 0.999. Thus, the retrained model’s residual recognition depends strongly on the information in the supplied labels in these configurations.

Unlearning progress does not respond uniformly. On BANKING77 bundle 01, SimNPO reaches PℱP_{\mathcal{F}} of 0.60–0.61 under opaque labels, compared with 0.55–0.59 under semantic labels. On bundle 02, progress decreases from 0.70 to 0.45 at seed 17 and from 0.47 to 0.40 at seed 42. CLINC150 progress changes from 0.22 to 0.28 on bundle 02, from 0.22 to 0.13 on bundle 03, and from -0.24 to 0.02 on bundle 06. The last opaque run is statistically accepted but reproduces only a small fraction of the deletion shift.

The intervention therefore changes the oracle more consistently than it improves approximation to the oracle. Removing semantic labels does not by itself resolve CLINC150’s unlearning difficulty. These are mechanistic contrasts, including previously inspected targets, rather than an independent estimate of cross-target success.

5.3 Candidate composition changes both recognition and fidelity

We next rescore the existing checkpoints under the full option set (S0S_{0}), the set of forgotten classes with semantic neighbors (S1S_{1}), and the set of forgotten classes with randomly retained distractors (S2S_{2}). The two reduced schemas have equal cardinality, with 12 options in BANKING77 and 24 in CLINC150. This comparison controls for subset size between S1S_{1} and S2S_{2}. Comparison with S0S_{0} changes both size and composition.

For semantic BANKING77 bundle 01, Qwen3.5-0.8B’s oracle accuracy on ℱ\mathcal{F} increases from 0.269 under S0S_{0} to 0.460 under S1S_{1} and 0.799 under S2S_{2}. On 𝒢\mathcal{G}, the corresponding values are 0.306, 0.519, and 0.756. The deletion displacement on ℱ\mathcal{F} decreases from 0.608 to 0.438 and 0.148. SimNPO’s progress changes from 0.590.59 to 0.660.66 and then to 0.320.32. Other selected methods also lose progress with random distractors. Apertus-8B and Qwen3.5-9B retain positive row-level progress under S2S_{2}, although class-level uncertainty is wider (Figure 2C,D).

Opaque labels separate this effect from semantic oracle recognition. On BANKING77 bundle 01, oracle recognition remains near zero under reduced schemas, yet SimNPO progress falls from 0.61 under S0S_{0} to 0.00 under S1S_{1} and 0.12 under S2S_{2}. Bundle 02 shows the same qualitative failure to preserve full-schema progress (0.45 to 0.04 and 0.12). Reduced-schema sensitivity therefore persists even when the oracle does not substantially re-recognize the forgotten classes.

5.4 Reliable reference-model gains do not imply uniform transfer

In the reference class-deletion confirmation, SimNPO, GradAscent, GradDiff, and NPO satisfy the feasibility and gain criteria (Table 2). SimNPO has the largest point gains, Δ​ODℱ=0.359\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{F}}=0.359 and Δ​OD𝒢=0.280\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{G}}=0.280, while GradDiff-KL and Uniformization fail the utility/calibration gate despite positive distance gains. These results concern selected configurations, not an exhaustive ranking of optimization algorithms.

Across the reference model’s nine seed–bundle cells, SimNPO retains positive hierarchical gains on both views, remains feasible in every cell, and survives the stored leave-one-seed/bundle-out checks. Its pooled gains are 0.337 [0.238,0.443] on ℱ\mathcal{F} and 0.302 [0.208,0.412] on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. GradAscent does not yield positive aggregate gains, whereas GradDiff and NPO do, but both fail the full replication rule because feasibility is not maintained in every cell.

The frozen-setting panel contains 20 configurations, including the reference model. 19 satisfy the stored screening criterion, while Qwen3-4B is positive but unconfirmed. Progress on ℱ\mathcal{F} ranges from 0.20 to 0.63, with a median of 0.46. However, additional seeds reveal substantial variation (Figure 3). At seed 42, PℱP_{\mathcal{F}} is 0.17 for Apertus-8B, 0.14 for Qwen3.5-9B, 0.04 for OLMo-3-7B, and -0.18 for Qwen3-4B. The reference model retains 0.55. Results for seed 17 on bundle 02 are positive across all five replicated models. This purposive, incomplete panel supports within-model contrasts, not a population variance decomposition or a 95% general success probability.

Dataset transfer is less favorable. On CLINC150 bundle 01, the BANKING77 SimNPO settings increase oracle distance: gains are -0.191 on ℱ\mathcal{F} and -0.237 on 𝒢\mathcal{G}. Development tuning produces accepted results on bundles 02 and 03, but later bundles include unconfirmed and negative outcomes. Across 48 intents in six bundles, the pooled gains are 0.022 [-0.045,0.090] on ℱ\mathcal{F} and 0.022 [-0.044,0.094] on 𝒢\mathcal{G} (Table 3). These intervals do not establish a positive average effect across targets. They also do not establish equivalence to no-op. CLINC150 bundle 08 remains unused.

5.5 Suppression magnitude is insufficient to characterize fidelity

Let 𝒞ℱ⊂𝒞\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{F}}\subset\mathcal{C} be the forgotten classes and mM​(x)=∑c∈𝒞ℱpM​(c∣x;𝒮)m_{M}(x)=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{F}}}p_{M}(c\mid x;\mathcal{S}) their total probability mass. The suppression ratio

s=∑x∈ℰℱ∪ℰ𝒢[mMfull​(x)−mM𝒰​(x)]∑x∈ℰℱ∪ℰ𝒢[mMfull​(x)−mM𝒪​(x)]s=\frac{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}}}[m_{M_{\mathrm{full}}}(x)-m_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}(x)]}{\sum_{x\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}}\cup\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}}}[m_{M_{\mathrm{full}}}(x)-m_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}(x)]} (6)

compares the amount removed with the oracle’s amount. It is distinct from PvP_{v}, which uses the complete distribution.

Configurations selected to approximately match suppression on development data differ on held-out data (Figure 4). On BANKING77, SimNPO, GradAscent, and RMU yield s=s=0.78, 0.68, and 0.72, respectively, but Pℱ=P_{\mathcal{F}}=0.56, 0.55, and 0.04. Therefore, similar removal of forgotten-option mass does not ensure similar oracle fidelity. This comparison is approximate, since development matching does not enforce identical held-out suppression.

To describe distributional movement, define per-row changes ΔU=𝐩M𝒰−𝐩Mfull\Delta_{U}=\mathbf{p}_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}-\mathbf{p}_{M_{\mathrm{full}}} and ΔO=𝐩M𝒪−𝐩Mfull\Delta_{O}=\mathbf{p}_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}-\mathbf{p}_{M_{\mathrm{full}}}. Their projection gives

a\displaystyle a =⟨ΔU,ΔO⟩‖ΔO‖22,\displaystyle=\frac{\langle\Delta_{U},\Delta_{O}\rangle}{\|\Delta_{O}\|_{2}^{2}}, (7)
r\displaystyle r =ΔU−a​ΔO,\displaystyle=\Delta_{U}-a\Delta_{O},
‖ΔU−ΔO‖22\displaystyle\|\Delta_{U}-\Delta_{O}\|_{2}^{2} =(a−1)2​‖ΔO‖22+‖r‖22.\displaystyle=(a-1)^{2}\|\Delta_{O}\|_{2}^{2}+\|r\|_{2}^{2}.

The identity describes squared Euclidean error, not a decomposition of JS divergence. RMU’s pooled aligned coefficient is 0.40, compared with 0.67 for matched SimNPO. These diagnostics support a distinction between suppression and movement toward the oracle, and they do not identify a causal mediator.

On CLINC150, three settings near s=1s=1 on development data yield held-out ratios of 1.93, 1.61, and 1.18, with corresponding Pℱ=P_{\mathcal{F}}=-0.39, -0.17, and 0.17. Oversuppression and declining fidelity co-occur in this comparison. Increasing update strength is consequently not a general correction for weak progress.

5.6 Recovery depends on the starting checkpoint and the metric

Recovery uses BANKING77 bundle 01, training seed 17, with k∈{1,5,20}k\in\{1,5,20\} forgotten training examples per class and two adaptation seeds. We adapt the decision head and LoRA parameters (Hu et al., 2022) under matched settings and evaluate at t∈{0,1,5,10,25}t\in\{0,1,5,10,25\} updates on 160 unseen rows from four forgotten classes. Let p¯M​(t)\bar{p}_{M}(t) be the mean gold probability. Normalized trapezoidal area is AM=∑twt​p¯M​(t)A_{M}=\sum_{t}w_{t}\bar{p}_{M}(t), with weights (0.02,0.10,0.18,0.40,0.30)(0.02,0.10,0.18,0.40,0.30). Define

Gabs\displaystyle G_{\rm abs} =AM𝒰−AM𝒪,\displaystyle=A_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}-A_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}, (8)
Gadj\displaystyle G_{\rm adj} =[AM𝒰−p¯M𝒰​(0)]−[AM𝒪−p¯M𝒪​(0)],\displaystyle=[A_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}-\bar{p}_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}(0)]-[A_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}-\bar{p}_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}(0)],
HM\displaystyle H_{M} =AM−p¯M​(0)1−p¯M​(0),GH=HM𝒰−HM𝒪.\displaystyle=\frac{A_{M}-\bar{p}_{M}(0)}{1-\bar{p}_{M}(0)},\qquad G_{H}=H_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}-H_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}.

Hence Gabs=Δ​p¯​(0)+GadjG_{\rm abs}=\Delta\bar{p}(0)+G_{\rm adj}, where Δ​p¯​(0)=p¯M𝒰​(0)−p¯M𝒪​(0)\Delta\bar{p}(0)=\bar{p}_{M_{\mathcal{U}}}(0)-\bar{p}_{M_{\mathcal{O}}}(0). Headroom normalization is a secondary sensitivity analysis and does not identify an intrinsic learning rate.

Apertus-8B starts below its oracle (0.326 versus 0.429) but has positive baseline-adjusted recovery in every configuration, with pooled Gadj≈G_{\rm adj}\approx0.16 [0.12,0.20]. The advantage also survives headroom normalization. Its adjusted recovery exceeds a retained label-swap control by approximately 0.18 [0.14,0.22], with a class-bootstrap interval of [0.08,0.27] (Figure 5). This specificity is relative to a control that overrides an existing label mapping and starts near zero gold probability.

For Qwen3.5-0.8B, pooled adjusted recovery is approximately 0.04 [0.00,0.09] and its contrast with the label-swap control is -0.02 [-0.06,0.03]. The controls therefore do not establish forgotten-target specificity for this model. Neither control model shows a clear seen-row advantage over unseen rows; this is not an equivalence result.

Qwen3.5-9B starts above its oracle (0.614 versus 0.477). Its positive absolute area contrast coexists with a negative adjusted contrast of approximately -0.05 and a positive headroom-normalized contrast of approximately 0.10. Its apparent recovery advantage therefore depends on the endpoint. No specificity controls were run for this model.

Finally, new heads trained on retained classes atop frozen backbones give higher forgotten-class accuracy point estimates for unlearned classes than oracle backbones. Initialization-level variation and broad class intervals limit this evidence. Because semantic labels remain available, the experiment measures transfer through the frozen representations under this interface, and it does not demonstrate extractable deleted records.

6 Discussion and Limitations

The results support evaluating unlearning as an approximation to a specified counterfactual, including the decision schema. The oracle may retain substantial recognition through semantic labels; changing the offered alternatives can alter that recognition without changing model weights. Conversely, opaque labels can eliminate oracle recognition while leaving the unlearned model poorly aligned under a reduced option set. Therefore, a fixed-schema score does not establish that unlearning is robust to schema.

Three distinctions prevent stronger conclusions than the evidence supports. Statistical acceptance does not guarantee substantial progress, as illustrated by opaque CLINC150 bundle 06. A broad single-seed screen does not establish reliable transfer across training seeds or deletion targets. Higher recovery after adaptation does not, by itself, indicate faster learning, particularly when initial gold probabilities differ. The probability-geometry analysis is descriptive, and imperfect suppression matching does not isolate a unique mechanism.

The study is limited to two intent-classification datasets and supervised task adaptation from pretrained backbones. It does not establish erasure from pretraining, behavior in open-ended generation, or guarantees against privacy attacks. Granularity comparisons change the membership and organization of deleted rows and do not isolate granularity from every data-composition effect. A single label-code map per dataset cannot separate all consequences of changed label representations and training history. The architecture panel is purposively selected, recovery uses one trained seed per model, and class-bootstrap sensitivity is coarse with four forgotten classes. The retained label-swap control differs from forgotten-target adaptation in its initial difficulty and objective. Finally, checkpoint-level summaries do not recover the distribution over all possible retrained models.

7 Conclusion

We introduced DecisionUnlearn-Bench to examine how deletion changes probabilistic decision models and how well approximate unlearning reproduces those changes. Deletion granularity, label meaning, and candidate composition all affect the retraining target. SimNPO provides reproducible reference-model gains on BANKING77, but those gains do not transfer uniformly across seeds, targets, or datasets. Suppression and recovery diagnostics further show why low forgotten-class accuracy and high post-adaptation performance are insufficient summaries. Reporting the schema-specific oracle, absolute and normalized fidelity, retained utility, and controlled recovery yields a more precise account of what decision-model unlearning achieves.

Impact Statement

This work studies how to evaluate the removal of supervised training influence from probabilistic decision models. More accurate evaluation can help avoid unsupported claims that a model has forgotten private information. The experiments use intent-classification benchmarks and do not establish a privacy guarantee, successful record extraction, or the removal of knowledge acquired during pretraining. Recovery analyses are intended to characterize limitations of behavioral evaluation. Any release should respect the licenses of the datasets and base models and distinguish empirical fidelity results from guarantees about individuals’ data.

Appendix A Notation and Scope of the Retraining Reference

Throughout the manuscript, 𝒟ℱ\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}} is deleted training data, 𝒟R\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{R}} is retained training data, and ℰℱ,ℰ𝒢,ℰR\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}},\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}},\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{R}} are evaluation views. A deletion bundle is a fixed collection of target units, not a collection of independently trained models. Training seeds index the construction of full and retain-only checkpoints; adaptation seeds index subsequent recovery runs; head seeds index fresh-head initialization. These sources of variation are not interchangeable.

The full model MfullM_{\mathrm{full}} and oracle M𝒪M_{\mathcal{O}} are both derived from the same pretrained initialization under the task-training procedure. The oracle is a reference for deleting supervised adaptation data. It may retain relevant pretrained information and information inferred from the retained task data or the option descriptions. Its residual recognition is therefore compatible with the specified retraining counterfactual. It is not, by itself, evidence that the oracle was trained on 𝒟ℱ\mathcal{D}_{\mathcal{F}}.

The schema 𝒮=(𝒞,ℓ)\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{C},\ell) includes both candidate membership and the textual information supplied about candidates. We suppress 𝒮\mathcal{S} in formulas when all models being compared use the same schema. An oracle trained with opaque labels is a different checkpoint from the semantic-label oracle. By contrast, changing the candidate set at evaluation reuses checkpoints and supplies them with a different schema.

The supplied plots use D0D_{0}, PℱP_{\mathcal{F}}, P𝒢P_{\mathcal{G}}, ss, aa, and GadjG_{\rm adj}; these symbols have the same meanings here. Source-table strings dOD_F and dOD_G are rendered as Δ​ODℱ\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{F}} and Δ​OD𝒢\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{G}}. A change in retained accuracy is reported in percentage points when explicitly marked pp; probability and ECE differences are on the [0,1][0,1] scale.

Appendix B Data, Target Construction, and Experimental Coverage

B.1 Datasets and deletion units

BANKING77 contains 77 banking intents (Casanueva et al., 2020). CLINC150 contains 150 in-scope intents, with an additional out-of-scope option in our interface (Larson et al., 2019). The benchmark uses the existing intent annotations. No inference about a person’s identity or private attribute is an evaluation target in this study.

Example deletion removes 5% of training rows. Association deletion removes sub-intent clusters from selected parent intents, leaving other training examples of those intents. The primary BANKING77 association bundle contains ten clusters, whereas the supplied replication tables contain six and eight clusters in bundles 02 and 03, respectively. Class deletion removes all training rows associated with the selected class. BANKING77 class bundles contain four classes, whereas CLINC150 class bundles contain eight intents.

Target eligibility is evaluated on full-model development predictions. Class targets require accuracy of at least 0.70 and gold probability of at least 0.50, whereas association targets have a 0.65 accuracy threshold. Selection proceeds in hash order among eligible targets at the primary seed. Targets are not reselected to make subsequent seeds favorable. This produces one documented exception, where the semantic Qwen3.5-0.8B at seed 42 has a development accuracy of 0.65 on transfer_timing in the BANKING77 bundle 02. The corresponding opaque configuration passes its acquisition check.

B.2 Evaluation populations

For the primary BANKING77 class bundle, ℰℱ\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{F}} contains 428 deleted training rows and ℰ𝒢\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}} contains 160 unseen rows. The reference model’s second bundle has 382 deleted training rows. Row counts can differ across model-specific bundle-02 records. Therefore, a shared bundle label is not sufficient evidence that every architecture used identical deleted rows. The supplied results preserve the observed counts.

For class deletion, ℰ𝒢\mathcal{E}_{\mathcal{G}} comprises unseen rows of the deleted classes. Association-level generalization uses unseen rows of the deleted clusters. At the example level, evaluation rows are associated with deleted training rows through a nearest-training-row relation. Retained utility is computed on retained evaluation rows from the same configuration.

B.3 Observed coverage and stages

The 20-model granularity panel contains 120 full/oracle evaluations across three deletion requests. These are evaluation records, not necessarily 120 separately trained checkpoints, because full models may be reused. The 21st configured model, InternLM3-8B, was excluded due to a checkpoint-reload reproducibility issue.

The class-method confirmation uses Qwen3.5-0.8B, seed 17, bundle 01. Four methods continue to nine seed–bundle cells, with seeds 17, 42, and 99 and class bundles 01–03. The broad frozen-setting panel contains the reference model plus 19 additional model configurations. Four additional models join the reference in the targeted seed/bundle comparison: Apertus-8B, OLMo-3-7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3.5-9B.

The label study contains seven semantic/opaque pairs: BANKING77 bundles 01 and 02 at seeds 17 and 42, and CLINC150 bundles 02, 03, and 06 at seed 17. The opaque bundle-06 result appears in the detailed tables despite a stale not-run entry in the supplied design table. CLINC150 bundle 08 remains reserved. The candidate-set study additionally includes opaque BANKING77 bundles 01 and 02.

The run registry contains 358 displayed records. Its footer reports 1,043 evaluation records in the wider collection, including 646 development-sweep candidates, eight development-reference records, and 31 synthetic fixtures. The omitted records are not independent experimental replications. Table S1 summarizes the registry, and its CSV companion preserves every displayed row, including shortened keys that are not globally unique. The complete source paths and granularity fields must accompany any public machine-readable release.

Appendix C Model Training, Methods, and Configuration Reporting

The study compares probabilistic decision checkpoints through their complete option distributions. Approximate unlearning begins from the full checkpoint, whereas the oracle is constructed by applying the task-training procedure to the retained data from the shared pretrained initialization. Recovery explicitly updates the decision head and LoRA parameters; fresh-head analysis freezes the corresponding backbone and replaces the head.

GradAscent reverses the supervised objective on deleted examples. GradDiff combines forgetting pressure with retained-data supervision, and GradDiff-KL uses a retained-distribution regularizer. NPO and SimNPO use preference-inspired forgetting objectives (Zhang et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025). RMU intervenes on representations (li2024wmdp). Uniformization is an erasure control. These descriptions identify the evaluated method families, and their exact decision-probability losses and implementation-specific normalization must match the released code.

The CLINC150 tuning figure identifies the selected configuration as learning rate 3×10−53\times 10^{-5}, β=10\beta=10, retained-objective weight α=0.5\alpha=0.5, and 10 epochs. Its development objective is approximately 0.641, versus 0.945 for no-op. The selected point lies on the tested grid boundary. The result is reported as the selected tested setting, without asserting that it is an optimum beyond the grid. Dataset tuning used the development bundle, and the subsequent semantic-label evaluations use frozen settings.

Recovery uses learning rate 10−410^{-4}, three exposure budgets, and two adaptation seeds. Conditional seed-42 strength diagnostics use learning rate 6×10−56\times 10^{-5} on Apertus-8B and Qwen3.5-9B. The exact frozen BANKING77 selection and all full/oracle/head-training settings are referenced by a configuration CSV in the original asset notes, but that CSV is absent from this archive.

Appendix D Metrics and Statistical Analysis

D.1 Distributional metrics

For distributions 𝐩,𝐪\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q} and 𝐦=(𝐩+𝐪)/2\mathbf{m}=(\mathbf{p}+\mathbf{q})/2,

JS2(𝐩,𝐪)=12KL2(𝐩∥𝐦)+12KL2(𝐪∥𝐦).\operatorname{JS}_{2}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{KL}_{2}(\mathbf{p}\|\mathbf{m})+\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{KL}_{2}(\mathbf{q}\|\mathbf{m}). (9)

Distances lie between zero and one. Numerical stabilization uses ϵ=10−12\epsilon=10^{-12}. Oracle distance is an average of row divergences. Normalized progress is a ratio of aggregate distances, not an average of row-wise progress ratios. Each schema and label condition uses its own full/oracle denominator.

Retained accuracy uses the model’s highest-probability option. ECE compares confidence with empirical correctness within bins. The standard form is

ECER=∑j=1J|Bj||ℰR|​|Acc⁡(Bj)−conf⁡(Bj)|.\operatorname{ECE}_{\mathrm{R}}=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\frac{|B_{j}|}{|\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{R}}|}\left|\operatorname{Acc}(B_{j})-\operatorname{conf}(B_{j})\right|. (10)

The specific binning procedure is part of the implementation and must be documented; no new calibration transformation is applied to the JS probabilities for this draft.

D.2 Within-configuration inference

Paired resampling keeps full, unlearned, and oracle predictions aligned for the same evaluation rows. The default analysis uses 5000 bootstrap replicates and percentile 95% intervals. Class- or cluster-level resampling assesses sensitivity to the unit of deletion. With only four forgotten classes in BANKING77, these sensitivity intervals have limited resolution and do not characterize arbitrary new class selections.

Both-view acceptance is an intersection criterion: both Δ​ODℱ\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{F}} and Δ​OD𝒢\Delta\operatorname{OD}_{\mathcal{G}} must have positive point estimates and positive lower bounds, and the retained-utility constraints must hold. Positive, unconfirmed denotes positive point gains with at least one nonpositive lower bound. No benefit and infeasible are retained as distinct reported outcomes. Statistical acceptance is not an equivalence test and does not require PvP_{v} to exceed a practical-effect threshold.

The frozen confirmation family reports a one-sided intersection-union pp-value formed from the larger of the two view-specific values, followed by Holm adjustment across the candidate family. Screening decisions are uncorrected across model configurations. The reported pp-values and intervals retain their original roles, and we do not recompute them from rounded table entries.

D.3 Cross-bundle summaries

Reference-model Phase 2 uses stored hierarchical resampling over seeds, bundles, and deletion units. A method replicates under the protocol only if the aggregate lower bound is positive on both views, feasibility holds in every observed cell, and the result survives the specified leave-one-seed/bundle-out checks. Positive aggregate distance gains can therefore coexist with a failed replication decision.

For CLINC150, the pooled analysis averages seeds within each intent and considers 48 intents from six bundles. The intent-level estimate is not formed by selectively pooling successful bundles. On ℱ\mathcal{F}, the reported intent-bootstrap interval is [-0.045,0.090], and the bundle-then-intent interval is [-0.054,0.107] around the same point gain of 0.022. Both retain substantial uncertainty. Mean per-intent progress is omitted because some displacement denominators are small.

Appendix F Label and Candidate-Schema Interventions

Opaque rendering replaces every option name and description with a fixed code. The original map contains 77 codes for BANKING77 and 151 for CLINC150, including out-of-scope. Input utterances, target identities, option identifiers, and option order are unchanged. Forgotten options remain present, and their logits are not masked. The intervention is therefore a change in the information supplied by labels, together with the corresponding full/oracle training under that rendering.

Table S5 reports acquisition, oracle accuracy, forgotten-option mass, displacement, and progress. Rounded zero accuracy does not imply exactly zero option probability: scientific notation is retained for the mass values. The semantic/opaque effect is strong for oracle recognition, but SimNPO’s normalized progress varies with bundle and dataset. A single fixed code map per dataset leaves code-assignment variability untested.

Candidate schemas are fixed within a bundle. S0S_{0} supplies all options. S1S_{1} supplies the forgotten classes and two retained semantic neighbors per forgotten class, and S2S_{2} supplies the forgotten classes with the same number of random retained distractors. Observed subset cardinalities are 12 for BANKING77 and 24 for CLINC150. The exact membership lists and selection code should accompany the release.

All models are rescored under the reduced input schema. This is not slicing and renormalizing a stored full-schema vector. Table S6 reports both views and the new denominator. For example, semantic CLINC150 bundle 02 has D0,ℱ=D_{0,\mathcal{F}}=0.039 with random distractors, compared with 0.298 under the full schema. The smaller denominator changes the interpretation and uncertainty of normalized progress.

Appendix G Suppression and Probability Geometry

The suppression ratio aggregates forgotten-option mass over the relevant rows before dividing. A value s=1s=1 matches the oracle’s net amount of removed mass; it does not specify which retained options receive that mass or whether individual forgotten classes are suppressed similarly. A value above one indicates greater net mass removal than the oracle.

Development matching uses target s=0.6s=0.6 on BANKING77 and s=1s=1 on CLINC150. Table S8 preserves the observed development and held-out values, including configurations whose utility gate fails on held-out data. Uniformization has no feasible development checkpoint near the matched target and is absent from that comparison. The matched SimNPO configuration is distinct from the main confirmation checkpoint, so its Pℱ=P_{\mathcal{F}}=0.56 should not be substituted for the main confirmation value 0.59.

For row ii with ΔO,i≠0\Delta_{O,i}\neq 0, orthogonality gives

⟨ri,ΔO,i⟩=0,‖𝐩U,i−𝐩O,i‖22=(ai−1)2​‖ΔO,i‖22+‖ri‖22.\langle r_{i},\Delta_{O,i}\rangle=0,\quad\|\mathbf{p}_{U,i}-\mathbf{p}_{O,i}\|_{2}^{2}=(a_{i}-1)^{2}\|\Delta_{O,i}\|_{2}^{2}+\|r_{i}\|_{2}^{2}. (11)

Summing these per-row identities is exact. The pooled coefficient displayed in the figures is

a¯=∑i⟨ΔU,i,ΔO,i⟩∑i‖ΔO,i‖22,ρr=∑i‖ri‖22∑i‖ΔO,i‖22.\bar{a}=\frac{\sum_{i}\langle\Delta_{U,i},\Delta_{O,i}\rangle}{\sum_{i}\|\Delta_{O,i}\|_{2}^{2}},\qquad\rho_{r}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_{i}\|r_{i}\|_{2}^{2}}{\sum_{i}\|\Delta_{O,i}\|_{2}^{2}}}. (12)

The pooled a¯\bar{a} must not replace every aia_{i} in the exact summed decomposition. The matched-suppression table reports identity errors at or below 2.0×10−152.0\times 10^{-15} and no rows with zero oracle displacement. The wider diagnostic figure includes additional runs with a broader numerical error range.

The magnitude-only and residual-only JS diagnostics use probability vectors that are projected back onto the simplex. This projection and the nonlinear JS metric prevent interpreting them as an additive JS decomposition. Correlations between these diagnostics and progress also share underlying probability vectors. They are descriptive associations, not independent causal evidence about the optimization mechanism.

Appendix H Recovery, Controls, and Fresh Heads

H.1 Adaptation and numerical summaries

Full, SimNPO, and retrained checkpoints are adapted using the same exposure examples, update schedule, and evaluation rows within each recovery configuration. Exposure budgets are k=k=1,5,20 rows per forgotten class, and adaptation seeds are 0 and 1. Evaluation occurs at updates 0,1,5,10,25. Trapezoidal integration divided by the horizon of 25 yields weights 0.02,0.10,0.18,0.40,0.30. Consequently, each area has the same probability scale as a time-averaged gold probability.

Table S9 provides all 18 summaries across model, budget, and adaptation seed. Its configuration-level identity residuals are at most approximately 10−1610^{-16}. The six settings for each model share the same underlying trained checkpoints and four forgotten classes. They are not six independent replications of model training.

Shared row resampling preserves dependence across checkpoints, time points, budgets, and adaptation seeds wherever the same evaluation row is reused. Class intervals condition on the four tested forgotten classes and the reused backbones. Threshold times are the first evaluated update whose mean gold probability reaches the threshold; they are grid-based observations, not interpolated continuous crossing times. An unreached threshold is right-censored at 25 updates.

H.2 Starting point and headroom

Absolute area contains both the initial probability difference and the integrated difference in subsequent gains. Subtracting the initial value removes that additive offset. Headroom normalization instead asks what fraction of 1−p¯​(0)1-\bar{p}(0) is recovered. The principal headroom analysis uses a ratio of aggregate means; averaging row-level ratios yields a different estimand and can place large weight on rows starting near one. No equivalence between these aggregations is assumed.

Apertus-8B’s adjusted gains are positive across all configurations. Qwen3.5-9B’s adjusted gains are negative for every configuration, whereas its headroom point contrasts are positive. This metric dependence is part of the result rather than a basis for selecting one favorable summary. Neither adjustment alone identifies a model-intrinsic learning rate.

H.3 Specificity and exposure controls

Controls are available for Qwen3.5-0.8B and Apertus-8B. For an evaluation population qq, let

Rq=[AU,q−p¯U,q​(0)]−[AO,q−p¯O,q​(0)].R_{q}=[A_{U,q}-\bar{p}_{U,q}(0)]-[A_{O,q}-\bar{p}_{O,q}(0)]. (13)

The specificity contrast is Runseen−RswapR_{\rm unseen}-R_{\rm swap}; the exposure contrast is Rseen−RunseenR_{\rm seen}-R_{\rm unseen}. These are direct differences of paired advantages, not comparisons of whether separate intervals include zero.

In the retained label-swap arm, a retained class XX is relabeled as YY and adapted using the same budget and schedule. This arm starts with a near-zero target probability and reverses a previously correct mapping. Therefore, a positive specificity contrast establishes a difference relative to this particular control, not exclusion of all forms of general post-unlearning plasticity.

Seen evaluation rows belong to the original deletion set but are excluded from the new exposure. Figure S12 reports 4 exposed and 424 remaining seen rows for k=1k=1, 20 and 408 for k=5k=5, and 80 and 348 for k=20k=20, in both control models and adaptation seeds. The supplied audit reports verified disjointness. With no clear positive seen-minus-unseen advantage, these experiments do not establish a record-specific recovery effect; they also do not prove the absence of such an effect.

H.4 Fresh-head transfer

The fresh-head study freezes each backbone and trains a newly initialized decision head on retained-class rows, with three matched head initializations. The full backbone is a reference ceiling, and the oracle backbone is the counterfactual comparison. Figure S13 reports forgotten-class accuracy, gold probability, and retained accuracy separately for every initialization.

Higher forgotten-class recognition with an unlearned backbone can indicate distinct transfer properties, while semantic option labels remain available. The experiment does not isolate storage of individual deleted records. The supplied caption states that pooled row intervals exclude zero, whereas class intervals do not; the exact pooled fresh-head and control tables are not included in the archive, so the manuscript does not invent additional numerical interval bounds.

Appendix I Optimization Diagnostics and Conditional Strength Reruns

The seed comparison reveals several distinct patterns (Table S10). For Apertus-8B, suppression on ℱ\mathcal{F} falls from 1.07 to 0.39 between seeds 17 and 42; for Qwen3.5-9B it falls from 0.57 to 0.15. Their progress also falls. In OLMo-3-7B, suppression is much more similar (0.38 versus 0.35), while progress decreases from 0.34 to 0.04. For Qwen3-4B, suppression is 0.60 versus 0.61, but progress changes from 0.28 to -0.18. Therefore, insufficient suppression is not a complete explanation for all seed effects.

The recorded training logs provide forget loss, retain loss, and gradient norms. Initial gradient norms are not uniformly smaller for the weaker seed. Parameter-update norms were not recorded, and the figures do not reconstruct a historical trajectory that was never saved.

Conditional stronger-update reruns are exploratory. At learning rate 6×10−56\times 10^{-5}, the best displayed Apertus checkpoint reaches approximately Pℱ=0.42P_{\mathcal{F}}=0.42, whereas the Qwen3.5-9B trace reaches only approximately 0.19 and later oversuppresses. The displayed best epochs were chosen after observing these traces; they do not replace the frozen-transfer estimates or establish a validated adjustment rule.

Appendix J Compute, Integrity, and Reproducibility

Table S11 reproduces logged GPU-hour summaries by evaluation category. These totals are partial: full-model evaluations record zero and do not include the training time stored with the full checkpoint. The table also does not establish complete recovery-job accounting. We therefore do not report the sum as the study’s total training cost or infer an unlearning speedup over full retraining.

The supplied audit reports exact recomputation of oracle distance for 358 evaluations and point-estimate agreement for 252 bootstrap comparisons. It reports identical intervals when the number of bootstrap draws matches, and differences of up to 0.0075 for stored summaries of 2000 versus 5000 draws, without category changes. These are reported upstream checks; the current manuscript package contains figure/table exports, not the raw probabilities needed to repeat them.

The audit also documents repaired filename collisions between semantic and opaque analyses and between training seeds, a reporting-label collision between GradDiff and GradDiff-KL, and recovery reruns after out-of-memory failures. No repaired or post hoc results are treated as additional independent replications. The separate S2-Rank privacy experiment stopped at its acquisition gate and did not test the proposed attack; it provides no evidence of privacy robustness.
